title: When you can't A/B test on patients, you build a fake one to test on
summary: When you can't A/B test or roll back on real patients, you replace the live experiment with a simulated one — a hazard-enumerated LLM patient and LLM judge validated against clinicians.
takeaways: When rollback isn't an option because a bad call already reached a real patient, replace live A/B testing with hazard-enumerated simulation graded by an LLM judge that's itself validated against expert clinicians.

Ufonia's Dora agent, live across 20 UK hospitals for roughly 200,000 clinical calls, is tested against an LLM-played patient and judged by an LLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro) that matched or beat 10 expert clinicians on a labeled corpus.

Anterior hits the same real-patient-data constraint from the other side, generating synthetic records from decision-tree policies so eval labels are correct by construction instead of scraped from protected health data.

sources.title: Shipping AI to a Million Patients Without an A/B Test — Jared Joselowitz, Ufonia
Don't be data poor — Anuj Iravane, Anterior

body:
## What happened
In a talk published 2026-08-19, [Ufonia](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=McknwOzbmyg) engineer Jared Joselowitz described how the company ships Dora, a voice AI agent that phones patients for post-op follow-ups, without the usual "ship to 5%, roll back if it breaks" playbook. Dora has completed roughly 200,000 clinical calls across 20 UK hospitals, with contracts to reach a million patients in two years. Because giving clinical advice makes Dora a regulated medical device, Ufonia can't randomize patients into a worse variant or undo a call — a red dashboard means a patient was already harmed.

## Why it matters
Canary releases, A/B tests, and roll-back-on-regression all assume you can catch and reverse a bad outcome before it costs anything. In healthcare, or any domain where an agent's action is irreversible or its data is protected, that assumption breaks — evaluation has to happen entirely before deployment.

## How it works
1. **Enumerate hazards first.** Ufonia lists concrete failure modes — a missed red flag, a hallucinated answer, ignored patient distress — before writing a test.
2. **Simulate the patient.** A framework called Matrix runs an LLM "PatBot" as a scenario-conditioned patient against Dora; in a study, real patients often rated the simulated patient more realistic than a real one.
3. **Judge the transcript.** An LLM "BehJudge" (Gemini 2.5 Pro) grades each call pass/fail with reasons, hitting F1 0.96 on a 240-example clinician-labeled corpus — matching or beating 10 expert clinicians.
4. **Optimize, then stage rollout.** Automated prompt optimization (GEPA) tunes Dora against a clinician-weighted cost matrix that punishes missed red flags harder than false alarms; autonomy expands only as user testing, supervised evaluation, and monitored deployment each pass.

[Anterior](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XAsb7MIAzm8) hits the same wall from the data side: their eval sets need real patient charts, which are protected health information that can't be retained or reused. Their fix is sampling a label and reasoning trace from policies written as symbolic decision trees, so each label is correct by construction — about 90% of Anterior's eval data is now synthetic, and clinicians in blind review told real from fake only about 60% of the time.

> "You don't ship the model, you ship the evidence."

## The catch
Both approaches live or die on the simulator being honest: a PatBot or decision tree that misses a real-world edge case teaches the judge nothing. Ufonia traces every prompt and judge verdict back to a specific hazard, so a regression is traceable, not just visible.
